intro.title: Welcome to Laayoune — Desert, Ocean, and Saharan Culture
intro.p1: Capital of the Laayoune-Sakia El Hamra region, Laayoune sits where the Sahara meets the Atlantic. The city combines a modern, airy center, a Spanish-era church, Saharan craftsmanship, and easy access to sand dunes and ocean beaches.
intro.p2: Most visitors spend one or two days here: start at Mechouar Square and the craft center, visit the arts museum and the Spanish church, then head to the dunes for sunset or Foum El Oued for the ocean. Khnifiss Lagoon and Tarfaya make a great day trip to the north.

mechouar.title: Mechouar Square
mechouar.p1: Built for King Hassan II's visit in 1985, Mechouar Square is the civic heart of Laayoune. Its arcades open up wide perspectives, making it the natural starting point for any walk downtown.
mechouar.p2: Locals gather here in the evening: it's the ideal spot to people-watch, sip mint tea at a nearby café, and get your bearings before exploring other sites.
mechouar.tip: Visit at sunset or early evening, when the square is liveliest and the light softens the arcades.

spanish_church.title: Spanish Church (Cathedral of Saint Francis of Assisi)
spanish_church.p1: Located on Avenue Hassan II, the former Spanish cathedral recalls the era when Laayoune was founded under Spanish administration. Its distinctive silhouette stands out against the surrounding modern buildings.
spanish_church.p2: It is primarily admired from the outside and easily pairs with a visit to nearby Mechouar Square.
spanish_church.tip: Ask locally before planning an interior visit, as visitor access can vary.

arts_museum.title: Museum of Saharan Arts
arts_museum.p1: Located on Oum Saad Square, the museum offers an introduction to Saharan arts, crafts, and traditions, providing helpful context for everything you'll see in the city and surrounding desert.
arts_museum.p2: It is a compact stop, ideal to pair with the craft center before shopping for souvenirs.
arts_museum.tip: Opening hours can change—check with your hotel before heading over.

craft_center.title: Craft Center & Markets
craft_center.p1: Near Mechouar Square, the craft center brings together local artisans and stalls offering rugs, jewelry, leatherwork, and fabrics inspired by Saharan traditions.
craft_center.p2: The surrounding markets offer a glimpse into daily local life, from fresh produce to household goods.
craft_center.tip: Compare several stalls before buying and bargain courteously.

mosque.title: Laayoune Mosque & Minaret
mosque.p1: One of Laayoune's most photographed landmarks, the mosque and its minaret stand out against the desert sky, especially at sunset.
mosque.p2: Entry is reserved for Muslims, but the exterior and surrounding streets are well worth a brief stop.
mosque.tip: Dress modestly around places of worship and avoid blocking entrances during prayer times.

wadi.title: Sakia El Hamra Wadi
wadi.p1: The Sakia El Hamra wadi runs through Laayoune and gives the region its name. Its banks catch the late-day light, offering a peaceful contrast to the bustling center.
wadi.p2: Its water flow varies by season, changing the landscape from one visit to the next.
wadi.tip: Late afternoon is the best time for a walk and photos.

dunes.title: Laayoune Dunes (Ocean of Sand)
dunes.p1: Just a few kilometers from the center on the road to Dakhla, the Laayoune dunes stretch to the horizon—offering a taste of the Sahara without a long drive.
dunes.p2: Sunset walks, camel rides, and 4x4 excursions are the classic ways to enjoy them.
dunes.tip: Bring water, sunglasses, and a scarf, and avoid venturing into the dunes alone at night.

foum_el_oued.title: Foum El Oued: Beach & Corniche
foum_el_oued.p1: About 25 km west of Laayoune, Foum El Oued is the city's Atlantic outlet: a wide beach where the ocean's energy contrasts with the silence of the desert. The renovated, well-lit corniche has become a popular evening outing for families.
foum_el_oued.p2: Buses run in summer, while grand taxis remain the standard way to get there the rest of the year; cafés, campsites, and rental villas are available on site.
foum_el_oued.tip: Atlantic currents can be strong—ask locally before swimming.

el_marsa.title: El Marsa & Its Port
el_marsa.p1: El Marsa is Laayoune's port district, connected to the city by a road heading west to the ocean. Fishing boats, port activity, and fresh fish give it a completely different atmosphere from downtown.
el_marsa.p2: Beachfront hotels and seafood spots make it a practical alternative base if you prefer sleeping near the sea.
el_marsa.tip: Ask permission before photographing fishermen or port facilities, and stay clear of active docks.

khnifiss.title: Khnifiss Lagoon (Naïla)
khnifiss.p1: North of Laayoune toward Tarfaya, Khnifiss Lagoon (Naïla) is a protected wetland where the desert meets the Atlantic, famous for its birdlife, including seasonal flamingos.
khnifiss.p2: It is best visited as a day trip by 4x4 or with a local guide, combined with a stop in Tarfaya.
khnifiss.tip: Hire an experienced local driver or guide and bring plenty of water and fuel.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.desc: The Mechouar Square area is walkable; petit taxis cover city trips, grand taxis serve Foum El Oued, and a car or 4x4 with a driver helps for the dunes and Khnifiss Lagoon.

timing.title: When to Visit
timing.desc: The weather is mild from autumn to spring; favor late afternoon for the dunes and wadi, and evening for Mechouar Square and the Foum El Oued corniche.

q1.question: How long should I spend in Laayoune?
q1.answer: One full day allows you to see Mechouar Square, the Spanish Church, the craft center, and the museum; add a second day for the dunes, Foum El Oued, or Khnifiss Lagoon.

q2.question: What is Laayoune best known for?
q2.answer: Laayoune is the largest city in southern Morocco's Atlantic region, known for Mechouar Square, its nearby sand dunes, and the ocean beach of Foum El Oued.

q3.question: Can I visit Laayoune as a stopover on the southern route?
q3.answer: Yes—Laayoune is a natural stop on the long N1 highway between Tan-Tan or Agadir and Dakhla, and it has its own airport.

q4.question: Do I need a car in Laayoune?
q4.answer: Downtown sights can be visited on foot or by petit taxi, though a car, 4x4, or driver is much more practical for the dunes, Foum El Oued, and Khnifiss Lagoon.
